items.q: Which best describes the role of a hypothesis in concept learning?
options: It stores the final trained model weights
It represents a possible function mapping inputs to outputs
It lists all possible training examples
It encodes error during model evaluation
items.explain: A **hypothesis $h$ is a candidate function** $h : X \to \{0,1\}$ — one guess at the target concept. Concept learning is the **search through the hypothesis space $H$** for an $h$ consistent with the training data. Weights belong to parametric models; a hypothesis is the more general idea.

items.q: What does a version space contain during the learning process?
options: All incorrect hypotheses
All hypotheses consistent with the training examples
The most general hypothesis only
The most specific hypothesis only
items.explain: $VS_{H,D} = \{h \in H \mid h \text{ is consistent with } D\}$ — **every** hypothesis that fits the data seen so far. Find-S returns only the **single most specific** one; Candidate Elimination maintains the whole space via its $S$ and $G$ boundaries.

items.q: What happens to the hypothesis space in Candidate Elimination when conflicting examples are introduced?
options: G becomes more general
S becomes more general
The version space becomes empty
No change occurs
items.explain:
Positive examples push $S$ **upward** and negative examples push $G$ **downward**. With inconsistent (noisy or contradictory) data the two boundaries **cross**, leaving **no hypothesis consistent with everything** — the version space collapses to $\varnothing$.

This is the algorithm's honest failure mode: it cannot represent *'no hypothesis in $H$ fits'* any other way, which is why it needs **noise-free data and the target concept present in $H$**.

items.q: What best describes the inductive bias of the ID3 decision tree algorithm?
options: It prefers trees with maximum depth to fully fit the training data
It prefers randomly ordered attributes to ensure diversity
It prefers shorter trees, and places attributes with high information gain closer to the root
It builds trees without considering information gain
items.explain:
**Shorter trees are preferred, and attributes with high information gain sit closest to the root.** Note it is a **preference (search) bias**, not a restriction bias — ID3 searches the **complete** hypothesis space of all decision trees but explores it in a biased *order*.

Contrast **Candidate Elimination**, whose bias is a **restriction**: the target concept must lie in $H$.

items.q: Decision tree algorithms such as ID3 employ a greedy approach. What does this imply?
options: The algorithm builds all possible trees and chooses the best
It selects the attribute with the highest gain at each step, without backtracking
It stores all hypotheses in memory
It avoids using any inductive bias
items.explain: ID3 commits to the **locally best** attribute at each node and **never revisits** that choice. The consequence: it can settle on a **locally optimal but globally suboptimal** tree — a shorter tree may exist that ID3's greedy path never reaches. Building all possible trees is intractable, which is exactly why the greedy heuristic is used.

items.q: In the EnjoySport task, what does the hypothesis ⟨?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?⟩ represent?
options: The most specific hypothesis — accepts nothing
The most general hypothesis — accepts every instance
A hypothesis with one attribute unconstrained
An inconsistent hypothesis
items.explain: **`?` means *any value is acceptable*** for that attribute, so all-`?` accepts **every** instance — the **most general** hypothesis. Its opposite is $\langle\varnothing,\varnothing,\dots,\varnothing\rangle$, which accepts **nothing** and is where Find-S begins.

items.q: Why does Find-S examine only the positive training examples?
options: Negative examples are usually noisy
It assumes by default that all instances are negative unless its present knowledge shows them positive, so only positives can force a change
Negative examples are not available in concept learning
It processes negatives in a second pass
items.explain: Find-S starts at the **most specific** hypothesis, which already rejects everything. A negative example is therefore **already classified correctly** and can never force generalisation — only a **misclassified positive** can. Its output is still consistent with the negatives **provided** the target concept is in $H$ and the data is error-free.

items.q: What is the entropy of a collection in which all examples belong to the same class?
options: log₂(n)
items.explain: $Entropy(S) = -p_+\log_2 p_+ - p_-\log_2 p_-$. With $p_+ = 1$ and $p_- = 0$: $-1\log_2 1 - 0 = \mathbf{0}$ — a **pure** collection carries no uncertainty. Entropy is **maximal at 1** for a 50/50 split, and reaching 0 is exactly the **stopping condition** that makes a node a leaf.

items.q: Information gain of an attribute A is best described as:
options: The entropy of the attribute itself
The expected reduction in entropy caused by partitioning the examples on A
The number of distinct values A can take
The accuracy of a tree built using only A
items.explain:
$Gain(S,A) = Entropy(S) - \sum_{v \in Values(A)} \frac{|S_v|}{|S|}Entropy(S_v)$ — the **expected reduction in entropy** from splitting on $A$. ID3 picks the attribute with the **highest gain** at each node.

Known weakness: gain is **biased toward attributes with many values** (a unique ID would give maximal gain and a useless tree), which is what **Gain Ratio** corrects.

items.q: A decision tree achieves 100% training accuracy but performs poorly on test data. This is:
options: Underfitting
Overfitting
High bias
Correct behaviour
items.explain: **Overfitting** — the tree has memorised noise and idiosyncrasies of the training set rather than the underlying pattern. The formal statement: $h$ overfits if some $h'$ has **higher training error but lower error over the whole distribution**. Remedies: **pre-pruning** (stop early) and **post-pruning** (grow fully, then prune back).

items.q: A model that is too simple to capture the underlying pattern exhibits:
options: High variance, low bias
High bias, low variance
Low bias, low variance
High irreducible error
items.explain: **High bias, low variance** — underfitting. It makes strong, wrong assumptions and gives **consistently** poor predictions regardless of the training sample. The mirror case is **high variance, low bias** (overfitting): predictions swing wildly with the sample. Total error $=$ **bias² + variance + irreducible noise**.

items.q: k-Nearest Neighbours is described as a lazy learner because:
options: It has low accuracy
It defers all computation until a query arrives, simply storing the training data
It uses very few training examples
It cannot handle continuous attributes
items.explain: A **lazy** learner does **no work at training time** — it stores the data and does everything at query time. So training is $O(1)$ and **prediction is expensive**. An **eager** learner (decision tree, logistic regression) builds an explicit model up front: slow to train, fast to predict.

items.q: What is the effect of choosing a very large value of k in k-NN?
options: The decision boundary becomes more jagged and sensitive to noise
The decision boundary becomes smoother, and the model may underfit
It has no effect on the boundary
It guarantees higher accuracy
items.explain: Large $k$ **averages over more neighbours** ⇒ smoother boundary, **less variance, more bias** (underfitting; at $k = n$ every query returns the majority class). Small $k$ — especially $k=1$ — gives a **jagged boundary highly sensitive to noise**. $k$ is the bias–variance dial.

items.q: In a confusion matrix, precision is defined as:
options: TP / (TP + FN)
TP / (TP + FP)
(TP + TN) / total
TN / (TN + FP)
items.explain:
**Precision = TP/(TP+FP)** — of everything **predicted positive**, how much really was. **Recall = TP/(TP+FN)** — of everything **actually positive**, how much was caught.

Memory hook: precision's denominator is the **predicted** column; recall's is the **actual** row.

items.q: Why is accuracy a poor metric on a dataset where 99% of examples are negative?
options: Accuracy cannot be computed for imbalanced data
A classifier predicting 'negative' for everything scores 99% while detecting nothing
Accuracy always underestimates performance
Accuracy requires probability outputs
items.explain: The **majority-class baseline** already scores 99%, so accuracy conveys almost nothing about whether the rare class is found. Use **precision, recall, F1** or **AUC**, which focus on the positive class rather than raw agreement.

items.q: What does an AUC of 0.5 indicate?
options: A perfect classifier
A classifier no better than random guessing
A classifier that is always wrong
An undefined result
items.explain: AUC = the probability that the model ranks a random **positive** above a random **negative**. **0.5 is the diagonal — random guessing**; **1.0** is perfect. Below 0.5 means it is systematically *inverted* — and can be fixed by flipping its predictions.

items.q: Why is logistic regression called a classification algorithm despite the name 'regression'?
options: It regresses on the class labels directly
It uses a linear regression on the log-odds, then applies the sigmoid to output a class probability
The name is historically incorrect
It performs regression during training and classification at test time only
items.explain: It fits a **linear model of the log-odds**, $\log\frac{p}{1-p} = \mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{x} + b$, then the **sigmoid** maps that to a probability in $(0,1)$, thresholded at 0.5. So the *regression* is on the log-odds; the *classification* is the thresholding step.

items.q: Grouping customers by purchasing behaviour without any labelled outcome is an example of:
options: Supervised learning
Unsupervised learning
Reinforcement learning
Semi-supervised learning
items.explain: **Unsupervised** — there is **no target variable**, only structure to discover. The slides' own examples include *a subgroup of cancer patients grouped by gene-expression measurements* and *groups of shoppers based on browsing and purchasing histories*.

items.q: In Mitchell's ⟨P, T, E⟩ definition, what do the three symbols stand for?
options: Prediction, Training, Evaluation
Performance measure, Task, Experience
Probability, Theory, Error
Parameters, Threshold, Epochs
items.explain: *A computer program is said to learn from **experience E** with respect to some class of **tasks T** and **performance measure P**, if its performance at tasks in T, as measured by P, improves with experience E.* For checkers: **T** = playing checkers, **P** = % of games won, **E** = playing games against itself.

items.q: Which pair correctly distinguishes generative from discriminative models?
options: Generative models learn P(y|x); discriminative models learn P(x,y)
Generative models learn the joint P(x,y) and can generate data; discriminative models learn P(y|x) or the boundary directly
Generative models are always more accurate
Discriminative models require unlabelled data
items.explain: **Generative** models the **joint** $P(x,y)$ (or $P(x|y)P(y)$) so it can **synthesise new data** — Naïve Bayes, GMM. **Discriminative** models only $P(y|x)$ or the boundary itself — logistic regression, SVM. Discriminative usually wins on pure classification accuracy; generative gives you more (sampling, missing-data handling).

items.q: In a decision tree, what does a leaf node represent?
options: An attribute test
A class label or predicted output
A branch condition
The information gain of the split
items.explain: **Internal nodes test an attribute**, **branches are attribute values**, and **leaves carry the class label**. A path from root to leaf is one **conjunction** of attribute tests, and the whole tree is a **disjunction of those conjunctions**.

items.q: How does C4.5 handle a continuous-valued attribute?
options: It discards the attribute
It sorts the values and evaluates candidate thresholds, choosing the split point with the highest information gain
It rounds all values to integers
It replaces each value with the mean
items.explain: Sort the values, consider **thresholds midway between adjacent values whose class differs**, and pick the one maximising gain — turning a continuous attribute into a **binary test $A < c$**. Missing values are typically handled by distributing the instance **fractionally** across branches in proportion to the known values.
